They explained their choice by citing features of the face they had actually rejected.
They refused to explain why they had chosen the face.
They described features that appeared only in the face they had originally chosen.

questions.passage:
Text 1
Psychologist Leila Haddad tested bilingual and monolingual children in Beirut on tasks requiring them to ignore distracting information, such as naming the color of the ink a word is printed in while ignoring the word itself. The bilingual children responded faster. Haddad proposes that constantly managing two languages trains a general ability to control attention.

Text 2
Psychologist Bruno Ferreira reviewed dozens of comparisons like Haddad's. In small studies, bilinguals often outperformed monolinguals, but in large studies that matched the two groups closely on family income and parents' education, the differences mostly disappeared. Ferreira suggests that some reported bilingual advantages may reflect differences between the groups other than the number of languages they speak.
questions.question: Based on the texts, how would Ferreira (Text 2) most likely respond to Haddad's proposal in Text 1?
options: He would agree with it, since large studies consistently confirm a bilingual advantage.
He would argue that bilingual children perform worse on attention tasks than monolingual children do.
He would want to know whether the children in Haddad's two groups were closely matched on factors such as family income and parents' education.
He would claim that naming ink colors does not require ignoring distracting information.

  • Linguist Hine Tawhiri studied 50 Māori-speaking families and found that children who had attended a language nest were more likely to speak Māori at home as teenagers than children who had not.

questions.question: The student wants to present Tawhiri's findings in a way that accurately conveys the conditions under which the language nest effect appeared. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

Language nests, first opened in Aotearoa New Zealand in 1982, have since been adopted for Hawaiian and Inari Sámi, and Tawhiri found that children who attended Māori language nests were more likely to speak Māori at home as teenagers.
Tawhiri found that, in families in which at least one parent was learning Māori, children were more likely to speak Māori at home as teenagers.

Among the families Tawhiri studied, children who had attended a language nest were more likely than other children to speak Māori at home as teenagers—but only in families in which at least one parent was also learning Māori.
